Let $L_x,L_y>0$, let $N_x,N_y$ be integers at least $2$, and set $h_x=L_x/N_x$ and $h_y=L_y/N_y$. The rectangular grid nodes are $(x_i,y_j)=(ih_x,jh_y)$ for $0\le i\le N_x$ and $0\le j\le N_y$. The interior index set is $I_h=\{(i,j):1\le i<N_x,\ 1\le j<N_y\}$, and its boundary is the set of grid nodes with $i\in\{0,N_x\}$ or $j\in\{0,N_y\}$. A grid function is a real-valued function on all grid nodes; $X_{h,0}$ is the vector space of grid functions that vanish on the boundary.

For real vectors $v,w$ indexed by $I_h$, define the weighted interior inner product and norm by
$$
\langle v,w\rangle_h=h_xh_y\sum_{i=1}^{N_x-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N_y-1}v_{ij}w_{ij},\qquad \|v\|_h=\langle v,v\rangle_h^{1/2}.
$$
For full grid functions, the same notation applies to their restrictions to $I_h$; it gives a semidefinite bilinear form and a seminorm on all grid functions, and an inner product and norm on $X_{h,0}$.

The edge differences are $D_xv_{i+1/2,j}=(v_{i+1,j}-v_{ij})/h_x$ for $0\le i<N_x$, $1\le j<N_y$, and $D_yv_{i,j+1/2}=(v_{i,j+1}-v_{ij})/h_y$ for $1\le i<N_x$, $0\le j<N_y$. For a scalar coefficient $a$ sampled at face midpoints, write $a_{i+1/2,j}=a(x_i+h_x/2,y_j)$ and $a_{i,j+1/2}=a(x_i,y_j+h_y/2)$.

The divergence-form Dirichlet operator on interior nodes is
$$
(A_h^av)_{ij}=-\frac{a_{i+1/2,j}D_xv_{i+1/2,j}-a_{i-1/2,j}D_xv_{i-1/2,j}}{h_x}-\frac{a_{i,j+1/2}D_yv_{i,j+1/2}-a_{i,j-1/2}D_yv_{i,j-1/2}}{h_y}.
$$
For $a\equiv1$, this is the five-point Dirichlet Laplacian $-D_x^+D_x^- -D_y^+D_y^-$. The associated edge energy is
$$
E_h^a(v,w)=h_xh_y\left(\sum_{j=1}^{N_y-1}\sum_{i=0}^{N_x-1}a_{i+1/2,j}D_xv_{i+1/2,j}D_xw_{i+1/2,j}+\sum_{i=1}^{N_x-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N_y-1}a_{i,j+1/2}D_yv_{i,j+1/2}D_yw_{i,j+1/2}\right).
$$
The homogeneous scheme solves $A_h^av=f_h$ in $I_h$ with $v=0$ on the boundary. For Dirichlet data $g$, it solves the same interior equations with $v=g$ at boundary nodes. This definition specifies the rectangular Dirichlet stencil; it does not specify a Neumann or nonrectangular boundary closure.

derivations.claim: Fix an interior row $j$ and write $q_i=q^x_{i+1/2,j}$. Telescoping the horizontal contribution gives $h_xh_y\sum_{i=1}^{N_x-1}-(q_i-q_{i-1})w_{ij}/h_x=h_y\sum_{i=0}^{N_x-1}q_i(w_{i+1,j}-w_{ij})-h_y(q^x_{N_x-1/2,j}w_{N_x,j}-q^x_{1/2,j}w_{0,j})$. Summing this identity over $j$ gives the horizontal energy and its two boundary terms.

Let $v\in X_{h,0}$. For each interior row, $v_{ij}=\sum_{k=0}^{i-1}h_xD_xv_{k+1/2,j}$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|v_{ij}|^2\le (ih_x)\sum_{k=0}^{i-1}h_x|D_xv_{k+1/2,j}|^2\le L_x\sum_{k=0}^{N_x-1}h_x|D_xv_{k+1/2,j}|^2$. Summing with weights $h_xh_y$ and using $\sum_{i=1}^{N_x-1}h_x<L_x$ proves the displayed discrete Poincaré inequality.

Applying the same telescoping sum in each column to the vertical flux gives the vertical energy minus the top and bottom boundary terms. Adding it to step 1.1 proves the displayed two-dimensional identity, with all four boundary contributions present.
If $w$ vanishes at every boundary node, both boundary sums in step 2.1 are zero, so $\langle A_h^av,w\rangle_h=E_h^a(v,w)$.
Apply step 3.1 with $w=v$. The face lower bound gives $E_h^a(v,v)\ge a_0h_xh_y\sum_{j,i}|D_xv_{i+1/2,j}|^2\ge (a_0/L_x^2)\|v\|_h^2$ by step 1.2.

If $A_h^av=0$ for $v\in X_{h,0}$, step 4.1 forces $\|v\|_h=0$, hence every interior value is zero; the boundary values already vanish, so $v=0$. Thus the square finite-dimensional matrix is injective and therefore invertible.

For $A_h^av=f_h$, steps 3.1 and 4.1 imply $(a_0/L_x^2)\|v\|_h^2\le\langle f_h,v\rangle_h\le\|f_h\|_h\|v\|_h$. If $v=0$ the claimed estimate is immediate; otherwise divide by $\|v\|_h$ to obtain $\|v\|_h\le(L_x^2/a_0)\|f_h\|_h$, which is the asserted inverse-operator bound.

derivations.claim: Fix an interior node $(x_i,y_j)$ and write $x=x_i$, $h=h_x$, $A_r=A_r^x$, and $U_s=U_s^x$. Taylor's theorem with bounded third derivative for $a$ and bounded fourth derivative for $u$ gives $a(x\pm h/2,y_j)=a\pm ha_x/2+h^2a_{xx}/8+R_a^\pm$ with $|R_a^\pm|\le A_3h^3/48$, and $D_+u=u_x+hu_{xx}/2+h^2u_{xxx}/6+R_u^+$, $D_-u=u_x-hu_{xx}/2+h^2u_{xxx}/6+R_u^-$ with $|R_u^\pm|\le U_4h^3/24$, where $D_+u=(u(x+h,y_j)-u(x,y_j))/h$ and $D_-u=(u(x,y_j)-u(x-h,y_j))/h$.

Multiplying the coefficient and difference expansions yields, with $F_\pm=a(x\pm h/2,y_j)D_\pm u$, $F_\pm=au_x\pm h(au_{xx}+a_xu_x)/2+h^2(au_{xxx}/6+a_xu_{xx}/4+a_{xx}u_x/8)+R_F^\pm$. The absolute values of the discarded products are bounded by $h^3(A_0U_4/24+A_1U_3/12+A_2U_2/16+A_3U_1/48)+h^4(A_1U_4/48+A_2U_3/48+A_3U_2/96)+h^5(A_2U_4/192+A_3U_3/288)+h^6A_3U_4/1152$. Since $h\le L_x$, this is at most $C_xh^3$ for the stated $C_x$.

The coefficient of $h^2$ in step 2.1 is the same for $F_+$ and $F_-$, so it cancels on subtraction. Thus $|(F_+-F_-)/h-\partial_x(a\partial_xu)(x_i,y_j)|\le(|R_F^+|+|R_F^-|)/h\le2C_xh_x^2$, because $\partial_x(a\partial_xu)=a_xu_x+au_{xx}$. Interchanging $x$ and $y$ proves the corresponding vertical-flux bound $2C_yh_y^2$.

By [F1], $A_h^au^*$ is the negative sum of the two discrete flux divergences. The continuous right-hand side $f$ is the negative sum of the matching derivatives. Subtracting these expressions and applying the horizontal and vertical bounds from step 3.1 gives $|(A_h^au^*)_{ij}-f_{h,ij}|\le2C_xh_x^2+2C_yh_y^2$ at every interior node, including nodes whose stencil touches a boundary value.

derivations.claim: Write $u_h^*=(u(x_i,y_j))$ and seek $U_h=u_h^*+e_h$ with $e_h\in X_{h,0}$. The discrete equations are equivalent to $A_h^ae_h=f_h-A_h^au_h^*$ on the finite-dimensional zero-boundary space. By [F2], $A_h^a$ is invertible, so this equation has exactly one solution; hence the Dirichlet scheme has exactly one solution $U_h$.

Define $\tau_h=A_h^au_h^*-f_h$. Then the equation for $e_h$ is $A_h^ae_h=-\tau_h$, and $e_h=0$ at every boundary node because the scheme uses the exact sampled Dirichlet data. By [F3], each interior entry satisfies $|\tau_{h,ij}|\le 2C_xh_x^2+2C_yh_y^2$.
The weighted sum defining $\|\tau_h\|_h^2$ has $(N_x-1)(N_y-1)$ terms, so $h_xh_y(N_x-1)(N_y-1)\le L_xL_y$. Therefore $\|\tau_h\|_h\le\sqrt{L_xL_y}(2C_xh_x^2+2C_yh_y^2)$.

Apply the inverse estimate [F2] to $A_h^ae_h=-\tau_h$ and then use step 3.1. This gives the displayed error bound; the derivative constants do not depend on $N_x$ or $N_y$, so the error is $O(h_x^2+h_y^2)$.

derivations.claim: For the exact samples $u_i=x_i^2$, $D_h^+u_0=(h^2-0)/h=h$, whereas $u'(0)=0$. Thus the imposed Neumann row has residual exactly $h$.

Define $V_i=x_i^2+h(1-x_i)$. Then $V_0=h$, $V_1=h$, so $D_h^+V_0=0$; also $V_N=1$. Since the second difference of the quadratic part is $2$ and the second difference of the affine part is $0$, $-\delta_h^2V_i=-2$ at every interior node. Hence $V$ satisfies [A1].

If two grid solutions existed, their difference $d$ would satisfy $\delta_h^2d_i=0$ for $1\le i<N$, $D_h^+d_0=0$, and $d_N=0$. The recurrence says $d_i-d_{i-1}$ is constant in $i$; the forward boundary row makes that constant $0$, and $d_N=0$ then makes every $d_i=0$. Therefore the solution in step 1.2 is unique.
The error is $V_i-u_i=h(1-x_i)$. Because $0\le x_i\le1$, its maximum absolute value is $h$, attained at $i=0$. The boundary residual and global error are both first order in $h$.

derivations.claim: Set $x_i=ih$ and $\phi_i=x_i(1-x_i)/2$ for $0\le i\le N$. Then $\phi_0=\phi_N=0$, $-\delta_h^2\phi_i=1$, so $A_N\phi=\mathbf 1$, and $0\le\phi_i\le1/8$ because $x(1-x)\le1/4$ on $[0,1]$.

If $w_0=w_N=0$ and $A_Nw\ge0$ at every interior index, a negative interior minimum $w_k<0$ would give $(A_Nw)_k=(2w_k-w_{k-1}-w_{k+1})/h^2\le0$. Equality is then forced, so both neighboring values equal $w_k$; repeating this along the finite grid reaches a zero endpoint, a contradiction. Therefore $w_i\ge0$ everywhere.

The kernel of $A_N$ is zero: if $A_Nv=0$ and $v$ has a positive interior maximum, the equation forces both neighboring values to equal that maximum, which propagates to a zero endpoint; applying the same argument to $-v$ rules out a negative minimum. Thus $v=0$, and the square finite matrix is invertible.

Let $g$ be any right-hand side, let $v=A_N^{-1}g$, and put $M=\|g\|_\infty$. If $M=0$, then $v=0$. If $M>0$, $A_N(M\phi+v)=M\mathbf1+g\ge0$ and $A_N(M\phi-v)=M\mathbf1-g\ge0$; step 1.2 makes both grid functions nonnegative. Hence $|v_i|\le M\phi_i\le M/8$ for each $i$, proving $\|A_N^{-1}g\|_\infty\le\|g\|_\infty/8$.

citations.quote:
Let $L_x,L_y>0$, let $N_x,N_y$ be integers at least $2$, and set $h_x=L_x/N_x$ and $h_y=L_y/N_y$. The rectangular grid nodes are $(x_i,y_j)=(ih_x,jh_y)$ for $0\le i\le N_x$ and $0\le j\le N_y$. The interior index set is $I_h=\{(i,j):1\le i<N_x,\ 1\le j<N_y\}$, and its boundary is the set of grid nodes with $i\in\{0,N_x\}$ or $j\in\{0,N_y\}$. A grid function is a real-valued function on all grid nodes; $X_{h,0}$ is the vector space of grid functions that vanish on the boundary.

For real vectors $v,w$ indexed by $I_h$, define the weighted interior inner product and norm by
$$
\langle v,w\rangle_h=h_xh_y\sum_{i=1}^{N_x-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N_y-1}v_{ij}w_{ij},\qquad \|v\|_h=\langle v,v\rangle_h^{1/2}.
$$
For full grid functions, the same notation applies to their restrictions to $I_h$; it gives a semidefinite bilinear form and a seminorm on all grid functions, and an inner product and norm on $X_{h,0}$.

The edge differences are $D_xv_{i+1/2,j}=(v_{i+1,j}-v_{ij})/h_x$ for $0\le i<N_x$, $1\le j<N_y$, and $D_yv_{i,j+1/2}=(v_{i,j+1}-v_{ij})/h_y$ for $1\le i<N_x$, $0\le j<N_y$. For a scalar coefficient $a$ sampled at face midpoints, write $a_{i+1/2,j}=a(x_i+h_x/2,y_j)$ and $a_{i,j+1/2}=a(x_i,y_j+h_y/2)$.

The divergence-form Dirichlet operator on interior nodes is
$$
(A_h^av)_{ij}=-\frac{a_{i+1/2,j}D_xv_{i+1/2,j}-a_{i-1/2,j}D_xv_{i-1/2,j}}{h_x}-\frac{a_{i,j+1/2}D_yv_{i,j+1/2}-a_{i,j-1/2}D_yv_{i,j-1/2}}{h_y}.
$$
For $a\equiv1$, this is the five-point Dirichlet Laplacian $-D_x^+D_x^- -D_y^+D_y^-$. The associated edge energy is
$$
E_h^a(v,w)=h_xh_y\left(\sum_{j=1}^{N_y-1}\sum_{i=0}^{N_x-1}a_{i+1/2,j}D_xv_{i+1/2,j}D_xw_{i+1/2,j}+\sum_{i=1}^{N_x-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N_y-1}a_{i,j+1/2}D_yv_{i,j+1/2}D_yw_{i,j+1/2}\right).
$$
The homogeneous scheme solves $A_h^av=f_h$ in $I_h$ with $v=0$ on the boundary. For Dirichlet data $g$, it solves the same interior equations with $v=g$ at boundary nodes. This definition specifies the rectangular Dirichlet stencil; it does not specify a Neumann or nonrectangular boundary closure.

derivations.claim: At $x=x_i$ and $h=h_x$, the two midpoint coefficients are $a_+=1+(x+h/2)^2$ and $a_-=1+(x-h/2)^2$, while the one-sided differences of $x^2$ are $D_+u=2x+h$ and $D_-u=2x-h$. Therefore $D_h^\mathrm{flux}u=(a_+(2x+h)-a_-(2x-h))/h=2+6x^2+h^2/2$.

The centered differences are $\delta_{x,h}^2u=2$ and $D_{x,h}^0u=2x$, while $a(x,y)=1+x^2$ and $a_x(x,y)=2x$. Hence $D_h^\mathrm{expanded}u=2(1+x^2)+(2x)(2x)=2+6x^2$, so subtracting from step 1.1 gives exactly $h_x^2/2$.

On the grid of [[def-rectangular-grid-and-dirichlet-flux-stencil]], put $q^x_{i+1/2,j}=a_{i+1/2,j}D_xv_{i+1/2,j}$ and $q^y_{i,j+1/2}=a_{i,j+1/2}D_yv_{i,j+1/2}$. For any grid functions $v,w$,
$$
\langle A_h^av,w\rangle_h=E_h^a(v,w)-h_y\sum_{j=1}^{N_y-1}\left(q^x_{N_x-1/2,j}w_{N_x,j}-q^x_{1/2,j}w_{0,j}\right)-h_x\sum_{i=1}^{N_x-1}\left(q^y_{i,N_y-1/2}w_{i,N_y}-q^y_{i,1/2}w_{i,0}\right).
$$
In particular, if $w$ vanishes on the boundary, then $\langle A_h^av,w\rangle_h=E_h^a(v,w)$. For every $v\in X_{h,0}$,
$$
\|v\|_h^2\le L_x^2\,h_xh_y\sum_{j=1}^{N_y-1}\sum_{i=0}^{N_x-1}|D_xv_{i+1/2,j}|^2.
$$
If all horizontal and vertical face values satisfy $a_{i+1/2,j},a_{i,j+1/2}\ge a_0>0$, then the homogeneous Dirichlet matrix $A_h^a$ is invertible and
$$
\|(A_h^a)^{-1}\|_{\ell_h^2\to\ell_h^2}\le \frac{L_x^2}{a_0},
$$
where $\ell_h^2$ is the norm $\|\cdot\|_h$ on interior vectors. The constants are independent of $N_x,N_y$.

derivations.claim: For every interior node, $D_x^+D_x^-x_i^2=2$ and $D_y^+D_y^-(y_j^2)=2$; the other coordinate second differences vanish. Thus $(A_h^1u^*)_{ij}=-(2+2)=-4=f(x_i,y_j)$.
The sampled values $u^*_{ij}$ also satisfy the exact Dirichlet boundary rows, so they solve the full discrete system.
Any two discrete solutions have a difference in $X_{h,0}$ in the kernel of $A_h^1$. By [F2] that kernel is zero, so the solution is unique and equals $u^*$.
